extracted.intended_audience: practitioners and parties filing petitions, motions, and responses in PTAB AIA proceedings (IPR, PGR, derivation)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and filing petitions, preliminary responses, testimonial and documentary evidence, and related papers in PTAB AIA trial proceedings (IPR, PGR, derivation), and for understanding the Board's institution and discretionary-denial considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, well-organized arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should avoid submitting a repository of all the information that a judge could possibly consider, and instead focus on concise, well-organized, easy to follow arguments supported by readily identifiable evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation of an overwhelming number of issues tends to detract from the argument and can cause meritorious issues to be missed or discounted. Judges are familiar with general legal principles, so extended discussions of general patent law may be unnecessary unless the law is disputed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count compliance and abuse prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office provides practical guidance regarding compliance with word count limits and will generally accept a party’s certification of compliance except in cases of obvious abuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party need not go beyond the routine word count supplied by its word processor. Parties should not abuse the process (e.g., excessive words in figures/drawings/images, deleting spacing between words, excessive acronyms/abbreviations to circumvent word counts). Such abuse may lead to a brief not being considered. If a party believes it suffers prejudice from an alleged violation, it should raise the issue promptly and take reasonable steps to remedy before approaching the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim charts and word count treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may file a claim chart to explain what the petitioner believes a claim means in comparison to another claim, a reference, or a specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim charts can streamline identification of key claim features and their comparison to evidence. Claim charts submitted as part of petitions, motions, responses, oppositions, or replies count toward applicable word limits but are not required to be double-spaced. A claim chart from another proceeding submitted as an exhibit will not count toward word limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony must disclose underlying facts or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits expressing an expert opinion must disclose the underlying facts or data upon which the opinion is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Fed. R. Evid. 705; 37 C.F.R. § 42.65. Opinions without disclosing underlying facts/data may be given little or no weight (Rohm & Haas Co. v. Brotech Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and data — provide sufficient explanatory information
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on scientific tests or data (e.g., IR spectroscopy, HPLC), the proffering party should provide information that assists the Board in understanding the significance of the test or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In addition to the explanation required by 37 C.F.R. § 42.65, include any other information the party believes would help the Board understand significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining obviousness, the Board will review any objective evidence of nonobviousness proffered by the patent owner where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should present objective indicia (secondary considerations) when relevant; the Board will consider such evidence along with other obviousness factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition filing date – minimum procedural compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a filing date, the petition must meet certain minimum standards (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.106 and applicable statute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally the petition must comply with statutory standards for the requested proceeding (e.g., IPR requires complete petition with required fee and certificate of service). A complete IPR petition must certify that the patent is eligible for IPR and that the petitioner is not barred/estopped, identify the claims challenged and the specific basis for the challenge (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104, 42.106). Similar requirements apply for PGR and derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for statutory institution thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in a proceeding before the Board is a preponderance of the evidence standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific petition content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner must certify availability of the patent/application for review, that it is not barred/estopped, identify each challenged claim and statutory grounds, provide claim construction(s), and state the relevance of the evidence to the issues raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For IPR and PGR, a petitioner must also identify how the construed claim is unpatentable over the relevant evidence (37 C.F.R. §§ 42.104(b), 42.204(b), 42.304(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard used by the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard that would be used in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b) — i.e., the Phillips framework — for petitions filed on or after Nov. 13, 2018.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will construe claims based on the record of the proceeding, taking into account claim language, specification, prosecution history, and relevant extrinsic evidence as in Article III courts. Parties should point out specific portions of the specification, prosecution history, and extrinsic evidence they want considered and explain relevancy. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for any construction advanced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where claim language may be construed under § 112(f), a petitioner must provide a construction that includes both the claimed function and the specific portions of the specification that describe the structure, material, or acts corresponding to each claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may elaborate on why § 112(f) should or should not apply. A petitioner who chooses not to address § 112(f) risks failing to satisfy 37 C.F.R. § 42.104(b)(3). See Williamson v. Citrix Online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior claim construction determinations — consideration and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Any prior claim construction determination by a federal court or the ITC that is timely made of record in the proceeding will be considered by the Board and given appropriate weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-exclusive factors for weight include similarities between the records, whether the prior construction is final or interlocutory, and whether the terms are necessary to deciding issues. Submission of such determinations is mandatory under 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b) if they are relevant information inconsistent with a party's position and should be submitted concurrent with the filing that contains the inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedure for submitting supplemental information
rubrics_metrics.description: After trial is instituted, the Board's rules on supplemental information govern timing and procedures for submitting claim construction decisions and other supplemental materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party must request authorization from the Board to file supplemental information. If more than one month after institution, the motion must show why the information reasonably could not have been obtained earlier. Normally permitted if final oral hearing has not occurred; Board may permit later filing if not close to one-year deadline. Parties should submit prior claim constructions as soon as available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent owner preliminary response — filing period and permitted content
rubrics_metrics.description: For IPR and PGR, a patent owner may file a preliminary response within three months after the Notice of Filing Date Accorded to Petition to demonstrate that no review should be instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preliminary response may present arguments and supporting evidence (including testimonial evidence) such as: (1) statutory bar to petitioner, (2) asserted references not printed publications, (3) prior art lacks a material limitation, (4) prior art does not teach/suggest petitioner's combination, (5) petitioner's claim interpretation unreasonable, (6) for PGR §101 explanation of patent eligibility, (7) reasons to exercise Director's discretion to deny under §314 and/or §325(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of testimonial evidence submitted with preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimonial evidence is permitted with the preliminary response and may lead to cross-examination opportunities if a trial is instituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No negative inference if a patent owner declines to present testimonial evidence with the preliminary response. The weight afforded testimonial evidence will be decided case-by-case. If a patent owner withdraws testimony submitted with preliminary response, that declarant usually will not be subject to deposition on the withdrawn declaration; if not withdrawn, the declarant is usually subject to discovery and deposition in the ordinary course after institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replies to patent owner preliminary response
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may seek leave to file a reply to the preliminary response; any request must show good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to grant a reply and its scope rests with the panel and takes into account the facts of the case. The Board does not expect such replies will be granted in many cases due to the short time to decide institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of preliminary response and statutory disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may elect to waive the preliminary response to expedite proceedings; no adverse inference will be drawn. A patent owner may also file a statutory disclaimer of one or more challenged claims to streamline proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no challenged claims remain after disclaimer, the Board will terminate the proceeding. If some claims remain, institution decision is based solely on remaining claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of preliminary-response issues after institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a trial is instituted, the Board may decline to consider arguments set forth in a preliminary response unless they are raised in the patent owner response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent owner waives an issue presented in its preliminary response if it fails to renew the issue in its post-institution response (In re NuVasive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory thresholds for institution (IPR, PGR, Derivation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different statutory thresholds apply for instituting each type of proceeding: IPR (35 U.S.C. § 314(a)) requires a reasonable likelihood that petitioner would prevail on at least one claim; PGR (35 U.S.C. § 324(a)) requires that the petition, if unrebutted, would demonstrate it is more likely than not (>50%) that at least one claim is unpatentable; Derivation (35 U.S.C. § 135(a)) has particularity, one-year timing, oath, and substantial evidence requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'reasonable likelihood' standard is flexible; PGR can also be satisfied by raising a novel or unsettled legal question important to other patents. Derivation petitions must state with particularity that an earlier applicant derived the claimed invention from the petitioner’s inventor and filed without authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director's discretion and considerations in instituting review (General Plastic factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond statutory thresholds, the Board considers whether exercising the Director's discretion favors instituting or denying review, including whether the same or substantially the same prior art/arguments were previously presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General Plastic non-exclusive factors include: (1) whether same petitioner previously filed a petition on same claims, (2) whether petitioner knew or should have known of prior art at time of first petition, (3) whether petitioner had patent owner's preliminary response or Board decision from first petition at time of second petition, (4) time elapsed between discovery of prior art and filing second petition, (5) whether petitioner explains elapsed time between filings, (6) finite resources of the Board, (7) requirement to issue final decision within one year of institution. These factors are not dispositive and other reasons (e.g., parallel proceedings) may weigh against institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel petitions and multiple petitions guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: One petition should be sufficient to challenge a patent in most situations; multiple petitions against the same patent may raise fairness, timing, and efficiency concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing two or more petitions against the same patent, the petitioner should identify (in petitions or separate paper) a ranking of petitions for Board consideration and a succinct explanation of differences and why they are material and justify additional petitions. The Board encourages a table to show similarities/differences. A separate paper for this purpose is limited to 5 pages when filed with each petition. Patent owner may respond in preliminary response or separate paper (also limited to 5 pages). Multiple petitions are allowed in rare circumstances (e.g., many claims in litigation or priority-date disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of previously presented art/arguments under 35 U.S.C. § 325(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether to institute, the Director may take into account whether the same or substantially the same prior art or arguments were previously presented to the Office and may reject a petition on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to deny under § 325(d) is fact-dependent and balances petitioner's desire to be heard against patent owner's interest in avoiding duplicative challenges. The Board considers the efficient administration of the Office. Parties may wish to analyze similar factors when art presented was considered previously in examination, reexamination, reissue, or earlier petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Becton Dickinson non-exclusive § 325(d) factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-exclusive factors the Board has used when evaluating whether to deny institution under § 325(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include: (1) similarities and material differences between asserted art and prior art during examination; (2) cumulative nature of asserted art and prior art evaluated during examination; (3) extent to which asserted art was evaluated during examination; (4) extent of overlap between arguments made during examination and petitioner's reliance; (5) whether petitioner has pointed out sufficiently how the Office erred in evaluating asserted prior art; (6) extent to which additional evidence/facts in petition warrant reconsideration of prior art or arguments. These are not exclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and scope of Board's institution decision
rubrics_metrics.description: In instituting a trial, the Board will either institute as to all claims challenged and on all grounds in the petition, or institute on no claims and deny institution; the Board will not institute on fewer than all claims or all challenges in a petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trial is instituted, the Board generally will provide analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of all challenges in the petition to guide the parties. The Board retains discretion to deny the petition as a whole under §§ 314(a) and 325(d) even when some claims meet threshold standards. If deficiencies affect only part of a petition, the panel will evaluate whether denying the entire petition better serves efficient administration and integrity of the patent system (35 U.S.C. §§ 316(b), 326(b); 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.108; 42.208).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and use of statements from other proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may consider statements regarding claim construction or scope made by parties in other proceedings if timely made of record and the submitting party explains how they support or contradict proposed constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include prior claim constructions in district court/ITC and patent owner statements made in preliminary responses in prior AIA proceedings. Parties should point out specific statements, explain relevance, and provide supporting evidence. Each party bears the burden of providing sufficient support for constructions advanced. Submission rules (e.g., 37 C.F.R. §§ 42.51(b), 42.123, 42.223) and timing requirements apply.
